title: A Gene Is Longer Than Its Message

scenes.tts: Here is an imagined human gene with four exons and three introns. From the start of transcription to the end of its last exon, it runs 5,137 nucleotides. The finished mRNA carries only 737 of them. Where did the rest go? RNA polymerase two makes a primary transcript from a protein-coding gene. A primary transcript is not yet a message.
scenes.caption: Here is an imagined human gene with four exons and three introns. From the start of transcription to the end of its last exon, it runs 5,137 nucleotides. The finished mRNA carries only 737 of them. Where did the rest go? RNA polymerase II makes a primary transcript from a protein-coding gene. A primary transcript is not yet a message.
scenes.visual: A scale bar of the gene (four blue exons, three grey introns) labelled 5,137 nucleotides, a short 737 bar beneath it, question marks over the introns, then the label primary transcript, not yet a message.
scenes.narration: Here is an imagined human gene with four exons and three introns. From the start of transcription to the end of its last exon, it runs 5,137 nucleotides. The finished mRNA carries only 737 of them. Where did the rest go? RNA polymerase II makes a primary transcript from a protein-coding gene. A primary transcript is not yet a message.

scenes.tts: Three changes turn it into a message. First, a cap goes on the five prime end, when the RNA is only about 25 to 30 nucleotides long. The cap is a methylated guanosine, joined by three phosphates, and it blocks exonucleases. Near the other end, the signal A A U A A A guides a cut in the RNA. Then poly A polymerase adds adenosines without copying any DNA, so the tail is not in the gene.
scenes.caption: Three changes turn it into a message. First, a cap goes on the 5′ end, when the RNA is only about 25 to 30 nucleotides long. The cap is a methylated guanosine, joined by three phosphates, and it blocks exonucleases. Near the other end, the signal AAUAAA guides a cut in the RNA. Then poly(A) polymerase adds adenosines without copying any DNA, so the tail is not in the gene.
scenes.visual: Strip of three changes. The cap blob joins the 5 prime end with three phosphate dots; an exonuclease chip is blocked. A yellow AAUAAA marker and a cut line near the 3 prime end; a green run of A's grows past the end of the DNA line beneath.
scenes.narration: Three changes turn it into a message. First, a cap goes on the 5′ end, when the RNA is only about 25 to 30 nucleotides long. scenes.tts: Most human introns of the major class follow the G U, A G rule. G U sits at the five prime end of the intron, and A G at the three prime end. A third site inside the intron, the branch point, contains an adenosine. A small nuclear particle called U1 finds the five prime splice site by base pairing. U2 pairs with the branch point and leaves the branch A bulged out.
scenes.caption: Most human introns of the major class follow the GU-AG rule. GU sits at the 5′ end of the intron, and AG at the 3′ end. A third site inside the intron, the branch point, contains an adenosine. A small nuclear particle called U1 finds the 5′ splice site by base pairing. U2 pairs with the branch point and leaves the branch A bulged out.
scenes.visual: Zoom to one intron between two exons. Yellow GU and AG boxes mark its ends, an orange A marks the branch point, a teal U1 docks on GU, a teal U2 docks on the branch point and the A bulges out.
scenes.narration: Most human introns of the major class follow the GU-AG rule. GU sits at the 5′ end of the intron, and AG at the 3′ end. A third site inside the intron, the branch point, contains an adenosine. A small nuclear particle called U1 finds the 5′ splice site by base pairing. scenes.tts: Splicing is two steps. In the first, the branch adenosine attacks the phosphate at the five prime splice site. The upstream exon is freed, and the intron forms a loop with a tail, the lariat. In the second step, the freed upstream exon attacks the three prime splice site. The exons are joined, and the lariat is released.
scenes.caption: Splicing is two steps. In the first, the branch adenosine attacks the phosphate at the 5′ splice site. The upstream exon is freed, and the intron forms a loop with a tail, the lariat. In the second step, the freed upstream exon attacks the 3′ splice site. The exons are joined, and the lariat is released.
scenes.visual: The same exon, intron, exon. Step one: an arrow from the branch A to the GU end, the left exon comes free and the intron closes into a lariat. Step two: an arrow from the free exon to the AG end, the exons join and the lariat drops away.
scenes.narration: Splicing is two steps. In the first, the branch adenosine attacks the phosphate at the 5′ splice site. The upstream exon is freed, and the intron forms a loop with a tail, the lariat. In the second step, the freed upstream exon attacks the 3′ splice site. The exons are joined, and the lariat is released.

scenes.tts: Run it on the whole gene. Splicing removes intron one, intron two and intron three, and joins the four exons. The three introns add up to 4,400 nucleotides, and the exons add up to 737. The mRNA is shorter because the introns are gone. It also carries a cap and a tail that the gene never encoded.
scenes.caption: Run it on the whole gene. Splicing removes intron 1, intron 2 and intron 3, and joins the four exons. The three introns add up to 4,400 nucleotides, and the exons add up to 737. scenes.visual: The scale bar again, with its cap and tail. The three introns lift out as lariats labelled 900, 1,500 and 2,000; the exons slide together; sums 900 + 1,500 + 2,000 = 4,400 and 150 + 87 + 100 + 400 = 737.

scenes.tts: Change one base at a splice site, and the exon beside it is often skipped. Lose exon two, and 87 nucleotides go, which is three times 29. The frame is kept, and the protein loses 29 amino acids. Lose exon three instead, and 100 go, three times 33 plus one, so the frame shifts by one base. Keep this rule: the frame survives only if the length lost is a multiple of three.

scenes.visual: Exon 2 shown as 29 triplet boxes and skipped: the frame stays aligned. Exon 3 shown as 33 triplet boxes plus one red leftover base and skipped: exon 4's triplets shift by one base. The rule is written as the remainder test.
